claims.source: The neuronal injury in the hippocampus after SE has been suggested to be important because it is typically followed by chronic seizures (epilepsy) in rodents and humans, and has been suggested to cause the epilepsy (Falconer et al., 1964; Sloviter, 1994; Cavalheiro et al., 1996; Herman, 2002; Mathern et al., 2008; Dudek and Staley, 2012; Dingledine et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: Chronic seizures after pilocarpine-induced SE involve the temporal lobe.
claims.source: Chronic seizures involve the temporal lobe, so the type of epilepsy is called temporal lobe epilepsy (TLE).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about the pilocarpine model.

claims.claim: After pilocarpine injection, spontaneous intermittent seizures begin several weeks later and continue for the lifespan.
claims.source: Several weeks later, spontaneous intermittent seizures begin and continue for the lifespan (Scorza et al., 2009; Botterill et al., 2019; Lévesque et al., 2021; Whitebirch et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations describing the pilocarpine model.

claims.claim: SE increases adult neurogenesis.
claims.source: It is known that SE increases adult neurogenesis (Parent and Kron, 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claims.claim: SE triggers a proliferation of progenitors in the week after SE.
claims.source: SE triggers a proliferation of progenitors in the week after SE (Parent et al., 1997).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Parent et al., 1997.

claims.claim: Many GCs that are born in the days after SE die in subsequent weeks by apoptosis.
claims.source: Although many GCs that are born in the days after SE die in subsequent weeks by apoptosis, some survive.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about post-SE neurogenesis.

claims.claim: Young neurons that arise after SE and migrate into the GCL may suppress seizures by supporting the inhibition of GCs.
claims.source: Young neurons that arise after SE and migrate into the GCL may suppress seizures by supporting the inhibition of GCs because adult-born GCs in the normal brain inhibit GCs when they are young (Drew et al., 2016; Ash et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis based on cited research about young neuron function.

claims.claim: Newborn GCs in the GCL after SE can exhibit low excitability.
claims.source: In addition, after SE, the newborn GCs in the GCL can exhibit low excitability (Jakubs et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Jakubs et al., 2006.

claims.claim: Some neurons born after SE mismigrate to ectopic locations such as the hilus (hilar ectopic GCs).
claims.source: However, some neurons born after SE mismigrate to ectopic locations such as the hilus (hilar ectopic GCs), where they can contribute to recurrent excitatory circuits that promote seizures (Scharfman et al., 2000; Parent and Lowenstein, 2002; Scharfman, 2004; Scharfman and Hen, 2007b; Parent and Murphy, 2008; Scharfman and McCloskey, 2009; Zhan et al., 2010; Myers et al., 2013; Cho et al., 2015; Althaus et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by extensive citations to prior research.

claims.claim: Hilar ectopic GCs can contribute to recurrent excitatory circuits that promote seizures.
claims.source: However, some neurons born after SE mismigrate to ectopic locations such as the hilus (hilar ectopic GCs), where they can contribute to recurrent excitatory circuits that promote seizures (Scharfman et al., 2000; Parent and Lowenstein, 2002; Scharfman, 2004; Scharfman and Hen, 2007b; Parent and Murphy, 2008; Scharfman and McCloskey, 2009; Zhan et al., 2010; Myers et al., 2013; Cho et al., 2015; Althaus et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by extensive citations to prior research.

claims.claim: Mossy cells are a major subset of glutamatergic hilar neurons which are vulnerable to excitotoxicity after SE.
claims.source: Mossy cells are a major subset of glutamatergic hilar neurons which are vulnerable to excitotoxicity after SE (Scharfman, 1999; Sloviter et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claims.claim: During SE, mossy cells may contribute to the activity that ultimately leads to widespread neuronal loss.
claims.source: During SE, mossy cells may contribute to the activity that ultimately leads to widespread neuronal loss (Botterill et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Surviving mossy cells can be beneficial after SE because they inhibit spontaneous chronic seizures in mice.
claims.source: However, surviving mossy cells can be beneficial after SE because they inhibit spontaneous chronic seizures in mice (Bui et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bui et al., 2018.

claims.claim: A large subset of vulnerable hilar neurons co-express GABA and somatostatin (SOM).
claims.source: Another large subset of vulnerable hilar neurons co-express GABA and somatostatin (SOM; Sloviter, 1987; de Lanerolle et al., 1989; Freund et al., 1992; Sun et al., 2007) and correspond to so-called HIPP cells (neurons with hilar cell bodies and axons that project to the terminal zone of the perforant path; Han et al., 1993).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations describing these neurons.

claims.claim: HIPP cells normally inhibit GCs and have the potential to prevent seizures.
claims.source: HIPP cells are important because they normally inhibit GCs and have the potential to prevent seizures.
claims.evidence: This is based on established knowledge about HIPP cell function.

claims.claim: The preservation of hilar mossy cells and SOM cells was found in females primarily.
claims.source: Remarkably, the preservation of hilar mossy cells and SOM cells, and the reduction in chronic seizures, was found in females primarily.
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analyses showing significant effects in females but not males.

claims.claim: The sex difference may have been due to a greater ability to increase adult-born neurons in females than males.
claims.source: The sex difference may have been due to a greater ability to increase adult-born neurons in females than males, consistent with sex differences in Bax- and caspase-dependent cell death (Forger et al., 2004; Siegel and McCullough, 2011).
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation based on observed data and cited literature on sex differences in cell death.

claims.claim: Both increasing and suppressing adult-born neurons appear to reduce chronic seizures.
claims.source: Therefore, taken together with the results presented here, both increasing and suppressing adult-born neurons appear to reduce chronic seizures.
claims.evidence: This is a synthesis of the current findings with prior literature.

claims.claim: Suppressing adult-born neurons led to a reduction in chronic seizures because there were fewer hilar ectopic granule cells.
claims.source: Past studies suggested that suppressing adult-born neurons led to a reduction in chronic seizures because there were fewer hilar ectopic granule cells.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of prior research findings.

claims.claim: Cre+ mice had a shorter duration of SE than Cre- mice.
claims.source: The duration of SE was shorter in Cre+ mice compared to Cre- mice (Cre-: 280.5±14.6 min, n=11; Cre+: 211.4±17.2 min, n=14; Student's t-test, t(23)=0.30, p=0.007; Figure 1E2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative EEG data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 1E2.

claims.claim: The latency to the onset of the first seizure after pilocarpine injection was similar in Cre- and Cre+ mice.
claims.source: When mice with and without electrodes were pooled, the latency to the onset of first seizure was similar in both genotypes (Cre-: 47.2±4.8 min, n=27; Cre+: 45.3±3.9 min, n=28; Student's t-test, t(53)=0.3, p=0.761; Figure 1D1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 1D1.

claims.claim: Cre+ females had a shorter latency to the first seizure than Cre+ males.
claims.source: Thus, a two-way ANOVA with genotype (Cre- and Cre+) and sex (female and male) as main factors showed a main effect of sex (F(1,51)=4.31; p=0.043) with Cre+ females exhibiting a shorter latency compared to Cre+ males (Cre+ females, 34.3±3.4 min, n=15; Cre+ males, 57.9±5.6 min, n=13; Tukey's post-hoc test, p=0.026) but not other groups (Cre- female, 46.7±9.3 min, n=12; Cre- males, 47.4±4.4 min, n=15; all p>0.344; Figure 1D3).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of latency data shown in Figure 1D3.

claims.claim: The total number of chronic seizures were similar in Cre- and Cre+ mice when sexes were pooled.
claims.source: First, we analyzed data with sexes pooled (Figure 2C) and the total number of chronic seizures were similar in the two genotypes (Cre-: 22.6±3.0 seizures, n=18; Cre+: 21.3±1.6 seizures, n=17; Student's t-test, t(33)=0.15, p=0.882; Figure 2C1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative seizure data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2C1.

claims.claim: Cre+ females had approximately half the chronic seizures of Cre- females.
claims.source: Tukey's post-hoc tests showed that Cre+ females had ~half the chronic seizures of Cre- females (Cre- female: 44.6±10.2 seizures, n=7; Cre+ female: 22.6±2.0 seizures, n=9; p=0.004; Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative seizure data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2C2.

claims.claim: Cre+ males and Cre- males had a similar number of chronic seizures.
claims.source: However, Cre+ males and Cre- males had a similar number of chronic seizures (Cre- male: 16.1±1.6 seizures, n=12; Cre+ male: 19.9±2.7 seizures, n=8; p>0.999; Figure 2C2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative seizure data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2C2.

claims.claim: Cre+ female mice had approximately half the seizures per day as Cre- females.
claims.source: Cre+ female mice had approximately half the seizures per day as Cre- females (Tukey's post-hoc test, Cre- female: 2.1±0.5 seizures/day; Cre+ female: 1.1±0.1 seizures/day; p=0.004; Figure 2D2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative seizure frequency data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2D2.

claims.claim: Female seizure durations were shorter than male seizure durations.
claims.source: When separated by sex, a two-way ANOVA showed that female seizure durations were shorter than males (F(1,29)=12.42; p=0.001).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of seizure duration data.

claims.claim: Cre+ females had longer seizure durations than Cre- females when all seizures were analyzed.
claims.source: Post-hoc tests showed that Cre+ females had longer seizure durations than Cre- females (Cre- female: 33.2±0.7 s; Cre+ female: 39.3±0.6 s, p<0.001; Figure 2F2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative seizure duration data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2F2.

claims.claim: Males had little evidence of postictal depression but it was common in females.
claims.source: We found that males had little evidence of postictal depression but it was common in females (Figure 3), a sex difference that is consistent with greater spreading depolarization in females (Eikermann-Haerter et al., 2009; Bolay et al., 2011; Kudo et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: This is supported by EEG analysis data shown in Figure 3 and citations to prior research on sex differences in spreading depolarization.

claims.claim: The number and percentages of seizures with postictal depression were reduced in Cre+ females compared to Cre- females.
claims.source: When all chronic seizures were analyzed (n=274), the number and percentages of seizures with postictal depression were reduced in Cre+ females compared to Cre- females (Fisher's exact test, p=0.009; Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of postictal depression shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: All females showed more postictal depression than all males.
claims.source: There was a sex difference, with all females showing more postictal depression (108/154 seizures, 70.5%) than all males (17/120 seizures, 14.2%; Fisher's exact tests, p<0.0001, Figure 3B-C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3B-C.

claims.claim: Cre+ females had fewer days with ≥3 seizures than Cre- females.
claims.source: Cre+ females had fewer days with ≥3 seizures than Cre- females (Cre- females: 6.3±1.4 days; Cre+ females: 3.0±0.4 days; Tukey's post-hoc test, p=0.009; Figure 4D3).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of seizure clustering shown in Figure 4D3.

claims.claim: Cre+ mice had more DCX than Cre- mice immediately before SE.
claims.source: A two-way ANOVA with sex and genotype as factors showed a significant effect of genotype (F(1,9)=60.78, p<0.001) but not sex (F(1,9)=1.20, p=0.301; Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative DCX immunoreactivity data shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: Cre+ females had more DCX than Cre- females before SE.
claims.source: Post-hoc comparisons showed that Cre+ females had more DCX than Cre- females (p=0.001) and the same was true for males (p=0.003).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of DCX data.

claims.claim: The area fraction of DCX in the GCL/SGZ was significantly greater in Cre+ mice than Cre- mice after chronic seizures had developed.
claims.source: Representative examples of DCX expression in the GCL/SGZ are presented in Figure 5F and Figure 5E shows the area fraction of DCX in the GCL/SGZ was significantly greater in Cre+ mice than Cre- mice (Cre-: 3.1±0.4%, n=20; Cre+: 4.2±0.3%, n=17; Student's t-test, t(35)=2.13, p=0.041; Figure 5D1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative DCX data shown in Figure 5E and 5F.

claims.claim: Cre+ females had more DCX than Cre- females after chronic seizures had developed.
claims.source: There was a significant effect of genotype (F(1,33)=12.62, p=0.001) and sex (F(1,33)=11.68, p=0.002), with Cre+ females having more DCX than Cre- females (Cre- female: 1.8±0.3, n=7; Cre+ female: 3.8±0.4, n=9; Tukey's post-hoc test, p=0.015; Figure 5E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative DCX data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 5E.

claims.claim: DCX levels were similar between Cre+ and Cre- male mice after chronic seizures had developed.
claims.source: In contrast, DCX levels were similar between Cre+ and Cre- male mice (p=0.498, Figure 5E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of DCX data shown in Figure 5E.

claims.claim: Cre+ mice had significantly more hilar Prox1 cells than Cre- mice.
claims.source: Cre+ mice had significantly more hilar Prox1 cells than Cre- mice (Cre-: 19.6±1.9 cells, n=18; Cre+: 60.5±7.9 cells, n=18; Student's t-test, t(34)=5.76, p<0.001; Figure 6C1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative Prox1 cell counts shown in Figure 6C1.

claims.claim: Cre+ mice had more GluR2/3-expressing hilar cells than Cre- mice.
claims.source: The results showed that Cre+ mice had more GluR2/3-expressing hilar cells than Cre- mice (Cre-: 10.0±1.8 cells, n=10; Cre+: 17.0±2.0 cells, n=13; Student's t-test, t(21)=2.46, p=0.022; Fig. 7A1-3).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative GluR2/3 cell counts shown in Figure 7A3.

claims.claim: Cre+ females had more GluR2/3 cells than Cre- females.
claims.source: There was a significant effect of genotype (F(1,18)=4.95, p=0.039) with Cre+ females having more GluR2/3 cells than Cre- females (Cre- female: 8.0±2.0 cells, n=6; Cre+ female: 19.1±2.7 cells, n=8; Tukey's post-hoc test, p=0.011; Figure 7A4).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative GluR2/3 cell counts and statistical analysis shown in Figure 7A4.

claims.claim: GluR2/3-ir hilar cells were similar in Cre+ and Cre- males.
claims.source: GluR2/3-ir hilar cells were similar in males (Cre- male: 13.0±3.0 cells, n=4; Cre+ male: 13.6±2.5 cells, n=5; p=0.915; Figure 7A4).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative GluR2/3 cell counts and statistical analysis shown in Figure 7A4.

claims.claim: Cre+ mice had more hilar SOM cells than Cre- mice.
claims.source: Next, we measured SOM hilar cells in pooled data (females and males together). These results were analogous to the data for GluR2/3, showing that Cre+ mice had more hilar SOM cells than Cre- mice (Cre-: 2.1±0.5 cells, n=9; Cre+: 4.6±0.6 cells, n=11; Student's t-test, t(18)=2.95, p=0.008; Fig. 7B1-3).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative SOM cell counts shown in Figure 7B3.

claims.claim: Cre+ females had more SOM cells than Cre- females.
claims.source: However, Cre+ females had more SOM cells than Cre- females (Cre- female: 2.2±0.6 cells, n=6; Cre+ female: 5.1±0.6 cells, n=8; Tukey's post-hoc test, p=0.019; Figure 7B4), although only in dorsal DG (Figure 7B4) not ventral DG (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative SOM cell counts and statistical analysis shown in Figure 7B4.

claims.claim: Numbers of SOM cells were similar in Cre+ and Cre- males.
claims.source: Numbers of SOM cells were similar in males (Cre- male: 2.2±0.7 cells, n=3; Cre+ male: 3.3±1.8 cells, n=3; p=0.897; Figure 7B4) in both dorsal and ventral DG (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B-C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative SOM cell counts and statistical analysis shown in Figure 7B4.

claims.claim: Parvalbumin-ir cells were not significantly different between Cre+ and Cre- genotypes.
claims.source: Parvalbumin-ir cells were not significantly different between genotypes (Student's test, t(19)=1.76, p=0.095; Fig. 7C1-3).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative parvalbumin cell counts shown in Figure 7C3.

claims.claim: Cre+ female mice had less Fluorojade C staining in the subiculum than Cre- female mice.
claims.source: For females, a two-way ANOVA with genotype and subfield as factors showed a significant effect of genotype (F(1,14)=11.21, p=0.005) with a smaller area fraction in Cre+ mice than Cre- mice for subiculum (p=0.032) and a trend in CA1 (p=0.060; Figure 8D1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative Fluorojade C data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 8D1.

claims.claim: Males showed no significant differences in Fluorojade C staining between genotypes.
claims.source: Males showed no significant differences either in genotype (F(1,8)=0.02, p=0.872) or subfield (F(1,8)=0.16, p=0.698; Figure 8D2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative Fluorojade C data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 8D2.

claims.claim: The incidence of SE was significantly higher in unimplanted mice compared to implanted mice.
claims.source: The incidence of SE was significantly higher in the unimplanted mice when sexes and genotypes were pooled (Fisher's exact test, p<0.0001).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claims.claim: Genotype had no effect on the incidence of SE.
claims.source: Genotype had no effect on the incidence of SE (Unimplanted, p>0.999; Implanted, p=0.565).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of SE incidence data.

claims.claim: The total number of chronic seizures and seizure frequency were similar in implanted and unimplanted mice.
claims.source: The total number of chronic seizures (F(1,17)=1.33, p=0.265) and seizure frequency (F(1,17)=1.27, p=0.276) were similar, suggesting that implantation did not influence chronic seizures (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: There were no significant differences in mortality associated with SE or chronic seizures between groups.
claims.source: There were no significant differences in mortality associated with SE or chronic seizures. For quantification, we examined mortality during SE and the subsequent 3 days, 3 days until the end of the 3-week-long-EEG recording period, or both (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A). Graphs of mouse numbers (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B1) or percentages of mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B2) were similar: groups (Cre- females, Cre+ females, Cre- males, Cre+ males) were not significantly different (Fisher's exact tests, all p >0.05).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative mortality data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Power during SE showed no effect of genotype for any frequency range.
claims.source: Two-way RMANOVA with genotype and time as main factors showed no effect of genotype for any frequency range: delta (1–4 Hz, F(1,7)=1.61; p=0.245); theta (4–8 Hz, F(1,7)=1.75; p=0.227); beta (8–30 Hz, F(1,7)=1.65; p=0.240); low gamma (80 Hz, F(1,7)=0.29; p=0.174); high gamma (80–100 Hz, F(1,7)=0.17; p=0.689).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of power spectral data.

claims.claim: There was a significant effect of time on power for all frequency bands during SE.
claims.source: There was a significant effect of time for all bands (delta, p=0.003; theta, p=0.002, beta, low gamma, and high gamma, p<0.001), which is consistent with the declining power in SE with time.
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of power spectral data over time.

claims.claim: The timing of SE was not significantly different in females than in males.
claims.source: However, the timing of SE was not significantly different in females than in males (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative timing data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claims.claim: Postictal depression is often associated with spreading depolarization.
claims.source: In recent years the advent of DC amplifiers made it possible to show that postictal depression is often associated with spreading depolarization (Ssentongo et al., 2017), a large depolarization shift that is accompanied by depolarization block.
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ssentongo et al., 2017.

claims.claim: The sex difference in postictal depression is consistent with greater spreading depolarization in females.
claims.source: We found that males had little evidence of postictal depression but it was common in females (Figure 3), a sex difference that is consistent with greater spreading depolarization in females (Eikermann-Haerter et al., 2009; Bolay et al., 2011; Kudo et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: This interpretation is supported by citations to prior research on sex differences in spreading depolarization.

claims.claim: The shorter female seizures may have been due to truncation of seizures by spreading depolarization.
claims.source: Because females exhibited more postictal depression (see Figure 3), corresponding to spreading depolarization (Ssentongo et al., 2017), the shorter female seizures may have been due to truncation of seizures by spreading depolarization.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation based on the observed data and cited literature.

claims.claim: Cre+ females may have had longer seizures because they were protected from spreading depolarization.
claims.source: Cre+ females may have had longer seizures because they were protected from spreading depolarization.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation based on the observed data on seizure duration and postictal depression.

claims.claim: Clusters of seizures can have a substantial impact on the quality of life.
claims.source: Clustering is commonly manifested in consecutive days with frequent seizures. Clusters of seizures can have a substantial impact on the quality of life (Haut, 2015; Jafarpour et al., 2019) so they are important.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical research on seizure clusters.

claims.claim: In humans, clusters are defined as at least 3 seizures within 24 hr.
claims.source: In humans, clusters are defined as at least 3 seizures within 24 hr (Goffin et al., 2007; Jafarpour et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical definitions.

claims.claim: Prox1 is a common marker of GCs in the GCL.
claims.source: Prox1 is a common marker of GCs in the GCL (Pleasure et al., 2000; Galeeva et al., 2007; Galichet et al., 2008; Steiner et al., 2008; Iwano et al., 2012), and the hilus (Scharfman et al., 2007a; Hester and Danzer, 2013; Cho et al., 2015; Bermudez-Hernandez et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations describing Prox1 as a marker.

claims.claim: In past studies, hilar ectopic GCs have been suggested to promote seizures.
claims.source: In past studies, hilar ectopic GCs have been suggested to promote seizures (Scharfman et al., 2000; Jung et al., 2006; Cho et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claims.claim: There was a correlation between the number of hilar ectopic GCs and the number of chronic seizures in Cre- mice, suggesting more hilar ectopic GCs improved rather than worsened seizures.
claims.source: When Cre- and Cre+ mice were compared (both sexes pooled), there was a correlation with number of chronic seizures (Figure 6D1) but it suggested that more hilar ectopic GCs improved rather than worsened seizures. However, the correlation was only in Cre- mice, and when sexes were separated there was no correlation (Figure 6D3).
claims.evidence: This is based on correlation analysis shown in Figure 6D1 and 6D3.

claims.claim: Hilar ectopic granule cells had no consistent effect on chronic seizures.
claims.source: In light of these inconsistent results, it seems that hilar ectopic granule cells had no consistent effect on chronic seizures.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the inconsistent correlation data.

claims.claim: Epileptogenesis after a brain insult like SE is suggested to be due to the hippocampal damage caused by the insult.
claims.source: It has been suggested that epileptogenesis after a brain insult like SE is due to the hippocampal damage caused by the insult (Cavalheiro et al., 1996; Herman, 2002; Mathern et al., 2008; Dudek and Staley, 2012; Dingledine et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: Loss of hilar mossy cells and SOM cells has been suggested to be critical for epileptogenesis.
claims.source: Here, we examined the loss of vulnerable hilar mossy cells and SOM cells because they have been suggested to be critical (Sloviter, 1987; Cavazos and Sutula, 1990; Cavazos et al., 1994; Henshall and Meldrum, 2012; Huusko et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claims.claim: An antibody to GluR2/3 was used as a marker of mossy cells.
claims.source: An antibody to GluR2/3 was used as a marker of mossy cells (Leranth et al., 1996) and a SOM antibody for SOM cells (Leranth et al., 1990; Savanthrapadian et al., 2014; Botterill et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations describing the use of these markers.

claims.claim: GluR2/3+ hilar cells were not double-labeled with Prox1, suggesting they corresponded to mossy cells, not hilar ectopic GCs.
claims.source: We confirmed that the GluR2/3+ hilar cells were not double-labeled with Prox1, suggesting they corresponded to mossy cells, not hilar ectopic GCs (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by double-labeling data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: Having more GluR2/3-ir mossy cells could be a mechanism that allowed Cre+ females to have reduced chronic seizures compared to Cre- females.
claims.source: These results in dorsal DG also were obtained in ventral DG (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B-C). The data suggest that having more GluR2/3-ir mossy cells could be a mechanism that allowed Cre+ females to have reduced chronic seizures compared to Cre- females.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation based on the observed preservation of mossy cells in Cre+ females.

claims.claim: Equal numbers of GluR2/3 mossy cells in Cre+ and Cre- males could relate to their lack of protection against chronic seizures.
claims.source: Equal numbers of GluR2/3 mossy cells in Cre+ and Cre- males could relate to their lack of protection against chronic seizures.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation based on the observed lack of difference in males.

claims.claim: The ability to preserve more mossy cells and SOM hilar cells in Cre+ females could be a mechanism by which Cre+ females were protected from chronic seizures.
claims.source: Therefore, the ability to preserve more mossy cells and SOM hilar cells in Cre+ females could be a mechanism by which Cre+ females were protected from chronic seizures.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation based on the observed preservation of these cell types in Cre+ females.

claims.claim: Loss of parvalbumin-expressing cells has not been considered to play a substantial role in epileptogenesis in the past.
claims.source: These data are consistent with the idea that loss of parvalbumin-expressing cells has not been considered to play a substantial in epileptogenesis in the past (Sloviter, 1987; Sloviter, 1994).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claims.claim: Parvalbumin expression may decline even if the cells do not die.
claims.source: However, it should be noted that subsequent research has shown that the topic is complicated because parvalbumin expression may decline even if the cells do not die (André et al., 2001; Sun et al., 2007) and data vary depending on the animal model (van Vliet et al., 2004; Huusko et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to subsequent research.

claims.claim: Prior studies showed hilar and CA3 neurons are protected from cell loss in Cre+ mice examined 3 days after SE.
claims.source: In our previous study of Cre+ and Cre- mice (Jain et al., 2019), tamoxifen was administered at 6 weeks and SE was induced at 12 weeks (like the current study). We examined neuronal loss 3 days after SE, when neuronal loss in the hilus and area CA3 is robust in wild-type mice. There is also some neuronal loss in CA1 at 3 days but more at 10 days after SE. We found less neuronal loss in Cre+ mice in these three areas (Jain et al., 2019).

results.result: Conditional deletion of Bax from Nestin-expressing progenitors successfully increased adult-born neurons in the dentate gyrus. Tamoxifen was administered at 6 weeks of age, and 6 weeks later, Cre+ mice showed significantly more DCX-immunoreactive immature neurons than Cre- mice in both sexes before SE (C63, C64). After chronic seizures developed (2 months post-SE), Cre+ mice still had more DCX than Cre- mice overall (C65), but this effect was sex-specific: Cre+ females had significantly more DCX than Cre- females (C66), while DCX levels were similar between Cre+ and Cre- males (C67).
results.evaluation: The experimental manipulation is well-documented with appropriate controls (C5, C6). The DCX quantification data before SE (C63, C64) and after epilepsy development (C65-C67) are supported by statistical analyses and figures. The sex-specific effects are clearly demonstrated with appropriate two-way ANOVAs and post-hoc tests. The methodology for DCX quantification is described in detail in the Methods section.

results.result: Bax deletion had modest effects on status epilepticus (SE) characteristics. Cre+ mice had significantly shorter SE duration than Cre- mice (C50), but latency to first seizure was similar between genotypes when sexes were pooled (C51). When sexes were separated, Cre+ females had shorter latency to first seizure than Cre+ males (C52). Electrode implantation significantly reduced SE incidence (C79), but genotype had no effect on SE incidence (C80). Power spectral analysis during SE showed no genotype effects across frequency bands (C83), though power declined over time in all groups (C84).
results.evaluation: The SE characterization is supported by quantitative EEG data with appropriate statistical tests (t-tests, two-way ANOVAs). The finding of shorter SE duration in Cre+ mice (C50) is statistically significant (p=0.007). The confounding effect of electrode implantation on SE incidence (C79) is appropriately acknowledged and analyzed. Power spectral analysis (C83, C84) provides additional characterization, though it shows no genotype effects.

results.result: Increasing adult-born neurons reduced chronic seizure frequency specifically in female mice. When sexes were pooled, total seizure numbers were similar between genotypes (C53). However, when analyzed by sex, Cre+ females had approximately half the chronic seizures of Cre- females (C54, C56), while Cre+ and Cre- males showed similar seizure numbers (C55). This represents a major sex-specific protective effect (C10, C16).
results.evaluation: The seizure quantification is based on 3 weeks of continuous video-EEG recording with clear seizure definitions. Statistical analyses using two-way ANOVA with genotype and sex as factors are appropriate. The sex-specific effect in females is robust (p=0.004) with adequate sample sizes (Cre- females n=7, Cre+ females n=9). The lack of effect in males is also clearly demonstrated. This is a primary finding of the study.

results.result: Postictal depression was reduced in Cre+ female mice. Males showed little postictal depression while it was common in females (C59, C61), consistent with greater spreading depolarization in females (C86, C87). The number and percentage of seizures with postictal depression were significantly reduced in Cre+ females compared to Cre- females (C60).
results.evaluation: The postictal depression analysis is based on quantitative EEG measurements with clear operational definitions (>50% reduction in amplitude). The sex difference is striking and statistically significant (p<0.0001). The reduction in Cre+ females is also significant (p=0.009). The interpretation linking postictal depression to spreading depolarization is supported by appropriate citations (C86, C87).

results.result: Female seizures were shorter than male seizures overall (C57), but Cre+ females had longer individual seizure durations than Cre- females when all seizures were analyzed (C58). The authors interpret this as females having shorter seizures due to truncation by spreading depolarization (C88), and Cre+ females being protected from this truncation (C89).
results.evaluation: While the seizure duration data are statistically significant (C57: p=0.001; C58: p<0.001), the interpretation regarding spreading depolarization (C88, C89) is speculative. The study did not directly measure spreading depolarization (which requires DC amplifiers), only postictal depression. The causal link between protection from spreading depolarization and longer seizures in Cre+ females is inferred but not directly demonstrated.

results.result: Cre+ females had fewer days with ≥3 seizures (seizure clusters) than Cre- females (C62). Seizure clusters can substantially impact quality of life (C90), and in humans are defined as ≥3 seizures within 24 hours (C91). The authors note that results may have underestimated effects on intercluster intervals because some Cre+ females had only one cluster in 3 weeks (C125).
results.evaluation: The cluster analysis is based on a clinically relevant definition adapted from human studies (C91). The reduction in days with ≥3 seizures in Cre+ females is statistically significant (p=0.009). The acknowledgment of potential underestimation of intercluster interval effects (C125) is appropriate and demonstrates scientific rigor. However, the intercluster interval analysis itself was not statistically significant.

results.result: Cre+ mice had significantly more hilar ectopic granule cells (marked by Prox1) than Cre- mice (C68). This finding was unexpected because prior studies suggested hilar ectopic GCs promote seizures (C93). Correlation analyses showed inconsistent relationships between hilar ectopic GC numbers and seizure outcomes (C94), leading to the conclusion that hilar ectopic GCs had no consistent effect on chronic seizures (C95).
results.evaluation: The Prox1 quantification is well-documented with clear methodology and statistical support (p<0.001). The finding of increased hilar ectopic GCs in Cre+ mice is robust. The correlation analyses (C94) are appropriately conducted but show inconsistent patterns. The conclusion that hilar ectopic GCs had no consistent effect (C95) is reasonable given the data, though it contradicts prior literature. This represents an important unexpected finding.

results.result: Cre+ mice showed preservation of hilar mossy cells (GluR2/3+ neurons) compared to Cre- mice, with sex-specific effects. Overall, Cre+ mice had more GluR2/3+ hilar cells than Cre- mice (C70). This effect was significant in females (C71) but not males (C72). Double-labeling confirmed these were mossy cells, not ectopic granule cells (C99). The authors suggest this preservation could be a mechanism for reduced seizures in Cre+ females (C100).
results.evaluation: The GluR2/3 quantification is supported by immunofluorescence data with appropriate statistical analyses. The sex-specific effect is clearly demonstrated (females: p=0.011; males: p=0.915). The double-labeling control (C99) strengthens the interpretation that these are mossy cells. The mechanistic interpretation (C100) is reasonable given that mossy cell loss is implicated in epileptogenesis, though causality is not directly proven.

results.result: Cre+ mice showed preservation of hilar somatostatin (SOM)-expressing neurons compared to Cre- mice. Overall, Cre+ mice had more SOM+ hilar cells than Cre- mice (C73). This effect was significant in females (C74) but not males (C75), and was observed in dorsal but not ventral hippocampus. Loss of SOM cells has been suggested to be critical for epileptogenesis (C97). The authors propose this preservation could be a mechanism for seizure protection in Cre+ females (C102).
results.evaluation: The SOM cell quantification is supported by immunofluorescence data with appropriate statistics (overall: p=0.008; females: p=0.019). The sex-specific and regional (dorsal vs. ventral) effects are clearly documented. The interpretation linking SOM cell preservation to seizure protection (C102) is reasonable given the established role of these cells in inhibiting granule cells, though direct causality is not proven.

results.result: Parvalbumin-immunoreactive cells were not significantly different between Cre+ and Cre- genotypes (C76). This is consistent with prior literature suggesting parvalbumin-expressing cells do not play a substantial role in epileptogenesis (C103), though the authors note that parvalbumin expression may decline without cell death (C104).
results.evaluation: The parvalbumin quantification shows no significant genotype effect (p=0.095), which is clearly stated. The interpretation is appropriately cautious, acknowledging that lack of difference in parvalbumin immunoreactivity does not necessarily mean these cells are unaffected (C104). This serves as an important negative control showing specificity of the neuroprotective effects.

results.result: Cre+ female mice showed reduced neuronal damage in CA1 and subiculum at 10 days post-SE compared to Cre- females. Fluorojade C staining showed significantly less damage in Cre+ females in the subiculum (C77), while males showed no genotype differences (C78). This complements prior findings of protection in hilus and CA3 at 3 days post-SE (C105) and addresses delayed cell death in CA1/subiculum (C106).
results.evaluation: The Fluorojade C quantification is supported by appropriate methodology and statistics (females: p=0.005 for genotype effect; subiculum: p=0.032). The 10-day timepoint is well-justified for assessing delayed cell death (C106). The sex-specific protection in females is consistent with other findings in the study. The complementary nature with prior 3-day data (C105) strengthens the overall neuroprotection narrative.

results.result: Electrode implantation did not influence chronic seizure outcomes or mortality. Total seizure numbers and frequency were similar between implanted and unimplanted mice (C81), and there were no significant differences in mortality between groups (C82).
results.evaluation: These are important control analyses showing that the surgical procedure for electrode implantation did not confound the chronic seizure results. Statistical analyses are appropriate (two-way ANOVAs, Fisher's exact tests). This addresses a potential methodological concern since some mice were implanted before SE and others after SE.

results.result: The sex-specific protective effects may be due to sex differences in Bax-dependent cell death. Before SE, DCX levels were similar in Cre+ females and males (C126), but after epilepsy developed, Cre- females had less DCX than Cre- males (C127). Possible explanations include greater cell birth in males during epileptogenesis (C128), less programmed cell death in males (C129), or Bax-dependent cell death in females but Bax-independent in males (C131), consistent with sex differences in Bax and caspase-dependent cell death (C11, C47, C130).
results.evaluation: While the DCX data showing sex differences after epilepsy development are solid (C126, C127), the mechanistic explanations (C128, C129, C131) are speculative. The study did not directly measure cell proliferation, apoptosis, or Bax-dependent vs. Bax-independent cell death pathways during epileptogenesis. The interpretations are based on indirect evidence and citations to other studies. Additional experiments would be needed to definitively establish the mechanism.

results.result: The authors conclude that increasing young adult-born neurons before SE can protect against epilepsy (C108, C151), but acknowledge uncertainty about the mechanism. They suggest increased neurons before SE may lead to reduced SE duration and less neuronal damage (C110, C111), which could lessen epilepsy (C111). They also propose that protection of hilar neurons from excitotoxicity was critical (C147, C148), but acknowledge they lack direct proof (C109, C149).
results.evaluation: The main conclusion that increasing adult-born neurons reduces chronic seizures in females is well-supported by the data (C108, C151). However, the mechanistic interpretations are appropriately qualified as uncertain or speculative (C109, C112, C149). The study demonstrates correlation between increased adult-born neurons, neuroprotection, and reduced seizures, but does not definitively establish causality or mechanism. The authors' cautious interpretation is scientifically appropriate.

results.result: The results are surprising because both increasing (current study) and suppressing (prior studies) adult-born neurons appear to reduce chronic seizures (C48, C114). Past studies suggested suppression reduced seizures by decreasing hilar ectopic granule cells (C49, C145), while the current study shows increased adult-born neurons and increased ectopic GCs also reduce seizures (C146).
results.evaluation: This represents an important conceptual finding that challenges simple interpretations of adult neurogenesis in epilepsy. The comparison with prior literature (C17, C49) is appropriate and well-cited. The paradox is clearly stated (C48, C114) and the current findings are solid (C146). This suggests the relationship between adult neurogenesis and epilepsy is more complex than previously thought, potentially depending on context, timing, and preservation of other cell types.

results.result: The authors acknowledge study limitations including potential type II statistical errors in small subgroups (3-5 mice) when divided by genotype and sex (C143), and that female mice were not staged for estrous cycle (C144).
results.evaluation: These are appropriate acknowledgments of study limitations. The small sample sizes in some subgroups (C143) could indeed lead to type II errors (false negatives), though the significant effects detected in females suggest adequate power for the main findings. The lack of estrous cycle staging (C144) is a limitation for a study showing sex-specific effects, as hormonal fluctuations could influence seizure susceptibility and neurogenesis.

results.result: The authors used conditional deletion of Bax from Nestin-expressing progenitors via tamoxifen administration at 6 weeks of age to increase adult-born neurons, as measured by DCX immunoreactivity. Cre+ mice showed increased DCX compared to Cre- mice both before SE and after chronic seizures developed, with sex-specific differences emerging after epilepsy (Cre+ females had more DCX than Cre- females, but males showed no difference).
results.evaluation: The reviewer explicitly states that 'increased DCX alone (without birthdating with BrdU) could indicate increased survival of adult-born neurons, not proliferation or birth of newborn neurons per se' and notes that 'the dynamics of adult-born neurons (proliferation, differentiation, and/or survival) could be different in epileptic (pilocarpine-treated) animals.' The reviewer requests analysis of additional stages of adult neurogenesis beyond DCX to clarify what cellular process is actually being measured.

results.result: Mice with increased adult-born neurons (Cre+) exhibited fewer chronic seizures, with the protective effect primarily in female mice. Cre+ females had approximately half the chronic seizures and seizures per day compared to Cre- females, while males showed no significant difference between genotypes.
results.evaluation: The editor states this work 'provides solid data, contradicting previous studies on suppressing chronic seizures by reduction in adult-born neurons.' The reviewer acknowledges the study 'demonstrates that increasing adult-born neurons (not increasing adult neurogenesis because BrdU birthdating was not performed) before status epilepticus (SE) leads to a suppression in chronic seizures' and praises the 'stringent' EEG recording parameters and 'comprehensive' analysis of chronic seizures. The sex-specific finding is also highlighted as a strength.

results.result: Postictal depression was reduced in Cre+ females compared to Cre- females. Males showed little evidence of postictal depression while it was common in females, representing a sex difference consistent with greater spreading depolarization in females.
results.evaluation: The reviewer notes the 'comprehensive' analysis of chronic seizures which includes postictal depression as one of the examined parameters. No specific concerns are raised about these findings, and the EEG recording methods are described as 'stringent,' supporting the validity of these observations.

results.result: Female mice with enhanced adult-born neurons showed less neuronal loss of hilar mossy cells (GluR2/3+ cells) and somatostatin-expressing neurons compared to wild-type females or males. Cre+ females had more GluR2/3 and SOM cells than Cre- females, while males showed no genotype differences. The preservation of these cell types is proposed as a mechanism for seizure protection.
results.evaluation: The reviewers do not raise specific concerns about the histological quantification of hilar cell populations. The editor acknowledges this is 'important work' and the reviewer notes the study's comprehensive approach. The lack of critique regarding these cellular findings suggests acceptance of the data, though the mechanistic interpretation remains speculative.

results.result: Cre+ mice had significantly more hilar ectopic granule cells (Prox1+ cells in the hilus) than Cre- mice. Contrary to expectations from prior literature, the correlation analysis suggested that more hilar ectopic GCs were associated with fewer seizures rather than more, though the correlations were inconsistent. The authors conclude hilar ectopic GCs had no consistent effect on chronic seizures.
results.evaluation: The reviewer does not challenge the quantification of hilar ectopic granule cells or the unexpected finding that increased ectopic cells were associated with reduced seizures.
